questions.q: Checkout reads the payment provider's SDK response directly in twenty places. What goes wrong when the business switches to another provider?
questions.explain: Provider-specific shapes (status: "success", amount_kobo) leak into business logic. An adapter keeps them in one class, so the rest of the app speaks its own contract and a switch touches one place.
options: Nothing, because all providers use the same JSON
Every place that reads the old provider's shape must change, and until it does, successful payments can be treated as declined
The new provider refuses to work with old code

questions.q: Checkout was written for provider A. What does it print for provider B's successful payment?
questions.explain: B has no status field, so the check fails and the code falls through to "declined", reading a field B does not have either. No error is thrown: the bug is silent, which makes it worse.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: In the adapter pattern, who defines the contract (the port) that adapters implement?
questions.explain: The contract describes what checkout needs: charge, refund, succeeded or declined. If it copied one provider's API, the next provider would have to pretend to be the first one, and the coupling would be back.
options: Your application, in its own words, from what the business logic needs

questions.q: Why is reference (the order id) part of ChargeRequest, and not only something an adapter might add?
questions.explain: Idempotency is a promise that checkout relies on. Putting it in the contract, and testing it in the contract suite, makes every adapter keep it: the fake by remembering references, KoboPay through the Idempotency-Key header.
options: So the provider can show it on the bank statement
It is the idempotency key: every adapter must promise that the same reference never charges twice, so checkout can retry safely
Because the registry needs it to find the adapter

questions.q: What does this idempotent charge function print?
questions.explain: The second call for order 1001 returns the stored result without calling the provider. Two orders, two charges, however often each is retried.

questions.q: Which lifecycle method should check that the provider is reachable and the API key works?
questions.explain: initialize prepares external resources without starting work. Checking there turns a wrong key into a startup failure, instead of a failed payment for the first customer.
options: initialize(): prepare and verify, before any work begins

questions.q: What is the difference between stop() and dispose()?
questions.explain: A graceful shutdown does both, in order: stop taking work, wait for what is running, then release connections and timers. The lesson's KoboPay adapter waits in stop and aborts leftovers in dispose.
options: There is none; they are aliases
stop ends active work (no new charges, let running ones finish) but keeps resources; dispose releases everything for good
stop deletes the adapter from the registry; dispose does not

questions.q: KoboPay cannot refund through its API. Where should the adapter say so?
questions.explain: Capabilities are about the runtime: http, abortSignal, gracefulShutdown, edgeRuntime… TypeScript rejects refunds there (TS2353). Business features belong in the business contract, where checkout can read them.
options: In your own contract, such as features.refunds, because AdapterCapabilities only lists platform abilities and refuses unknown names

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Names are trimmed and lower-cased for registration and lookup, so any casing finds the adapter and getNames() shows the normalized form. The adapter object itself is stored untouched, so its name is still Payments.

questions.q: When should you use registry.require(name) instead of registry.get(name)?
questions.explain: A missing payments adapter is a configuration bug that should stop startup loudly. get fits optional adapters, where your code has a sensible path for "not there".
options: When the app cannot work without that adapter: require throws AdapterNotFoundError, get returns undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both adapters declare http. supports answers false both for a missing capability and for an adapter that is not registered, without throwing. requireCapability throws when the adapter exists but lacks the capability.

questions.q: One of two adapters fails to initialize. What does this print?
questions.explain: initializeAll tries every adapter, even after one fails, and then throws one AggregateError listing the failures. You see all broken adapters in one startup. It does not wrap the errors itself: an adapter that wants AdapterInitializationError throws it from its own initialize.
options:
email ready
AggregateError 1 no API key

email ready
AdapterInitializationError 1 no API key

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The overall status is the worst one reported. Only adapters with a health method are asked, so storage is not in the report at all, and it does not count as unhealthy either.

questions.q: An adapter's health check never answers. What does this print?
questions.explain: With timeout, the registry stops waiting and reports the adapter as unhealthy. A health endpoint must answer even when a dependency hangs; otherwise the load balancer's check hangs too.
options: unhealthy Health check timed out after 50 ms.
degraded Health check timed out after 50 ms.

questions.q: The SMS gateway is down. How many times is its health check called?
questions.explain: attempts is the total number of tries, not the number of extra ones. A check that throws counts as unhealthy, with the error's message, and unhealthy results are retried until the attempts are used up.

questions.q: In which order are the adapters torn down?
questions.explain: The registry tears down one adapter completely (stop, then dispose) before the next, in registration order, and empties itself. It does not reverse the order, so when one adapter depends on another, manage their order with @zudojs/lifecycle.
options: stop database, dispose database, stop payments, dispose payments 0
stop payments, dispose payments, stop database, dispose database 0
stop database, stop payments, dispose database, dispose payments 0
stop database, dispose database, stop payments, dispose payments 2

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: remove only forgets the adapter: its connections stay open, and the first SMS adapter is never disposed. removeAndDispose also stops and disposes it. Use the second when you replace an adapter at runtime, or you leak the old one.
options:
sms disposed
true 0
new sms disposed
true 0

questions.q: During disposeAll, one adapter's stop() throws. What happens to that adapter?
questions.explain: Skipping disposal would leave connections and timers with nothing holding a reference to release them. The registry disposes anyway and reports every failure once all adapters were handled.
options: It stays registered and is never disposed
Its dispose() still runs, the other adapters are torn down too, and the failure is reported in an AggregateError at the end

questions.q: A charge request times out. What should checkout tell the customer?
questions.explain: A timeout means "no answer", not "no charge". The provider may have charged the card. "Failed" invites a second payment, and a retry with a new reference could charge twice.
options: "We don't know yet; we will confirm", and then find out with a retry using the same idempotency key, a lookup by reference or the provider's webhook
Nothing; just charge again with a new reference

questions.q: Which request is safe to retry after a timeout without any extra protection?
questions.explain: Reading does not change anything, so doing it twice is harmless. Charging, refunding and sending a message all have effects, and may only be retried with an idempotency key the other side honours.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The timeout error keeps the limit in timeout and, like most adapter errors, has status 500 and expose: false. "Not supported" is a 501 whose message may be shown. isAdapterError recognises every class in the family and nothing else.
options:
Adapter "kobopay" operation "charge" timed out after 800ms. 800 500
501 true true false

Adapter "kobopay" operation "charge" timed out after 800ms. 800 504
501 true true false

Adapter "kobopay" operation "charge" timed out after 800ms. undefined 500
501 true true true

questions.q: KoboPay's DNS name does not resolve, so fetch fails before any response. Which error should the adapter throw from charge?
questions.explain: The request never reached the provider, so this is a connection problem, and unlike a timeout the charge certainly did not happen. AdapterNotFoundError is the registry's error for an unknown adapter name, not for a missing server.
options: AdapterConnectionError, with the network error as its cause

questions.q: Why do the adapter errors keep the original problem in cause instead of in the message?
questions.explain: Adapter "kobopay" operation "charge" failed. is the same for every such failure, so alerts can group them. The cause, such as "KoboPay answered 503", is what an engineer needs, and stays out of customer-facing responses.
options: Because messages cannot be longer than one line
The message is stable and safe to show or group by; the cause keeps the details (status, network error) for logs and debugging
Because cause is sent to the customer

questions.q: setUpPayments receives PAYMENTS_PROVIDER=stripe-ish. Why throw at startup instead of falling back to the fake?
questions.explain: Defaults that hide configuration mistakes are dangerous, and with payments they lose money. Unknown or missing settings should stop the app with a clear message before it takes any traffic.
options: Because the fake cannot be created twice
A silent fallback would run production against a fake provider that "charges" nothing; a loud startup failure is found in seconds
Because unknown values are always numbers

questions.q: ShopFlow moves from KoboPay to a third provider. Which files change?
questions.explain: Business logic depends on the contract, so it is untouched. The new adapter must pass the same contract test suite as the others before it goes live.
options: Checkout, the order service and every test
A new adapter class, and the composition function that chooses the adapter (setUpPayments); checkout does not change
Nothing; the registry detects the provider

questions.q: What makes the lesson's contract test suite valuable when a new adapter is added?
questions.explain: Swappability is a claim, and the contract suite is its proof. A new adapter that charges a reference twice fails the suite before it can charge a customer twice.
options: It tests the provider's own code
The same promises (exact amount, readable decline, one charge per reference, refund or a clear refusal) are checked for every adapter, so any of them can replace another

questions.q: What are createMockAdapter and createMockAdapterRegistry for?
questions.explain: A mock adapter takes the lifecycle hooks and health you give it, so a test can make one adapter degraded or failing on purpose and check how your code reacts.
options: Replacing the real provider in production
Testing code that works with the registry, such as a readiness endpoint, with adapters whose health and lifecycle you control
Generating adapters from an OpenAPI file

questions.q: The readiness endpoint answers 200 when payments is degraded and 503 when it is unhealthy. Why not 503 for degraded too?
questions.explain: Degraded is a reason to alert, not to stop serving. If all instances report not-ready at once, the load balancer has nowhere to send traffic.
options: Because degraded adapters cannot be detected
A slow provider still works; taking every server out of the load balancer would turn slowness into a full outage
Because 503 is only for database errors
Because degraded means the adapter is disposed

questions.q: Which is the best health check for a payment adapter?
questions.explain: A health check must not do real work: charging, even a small amount, costs money and may trip fraud checks. A cheap, read-only call with a time limit tells you whether the provider is reachable and fast.
options: Charge ₦1 to a test card every few seconds
Call a cheap endpoint such as the provider's status or health route, with a short timeout
Do nothing and always return healthy

questions.q: The app shuts down while a charge is in flight. What does the lesson's KoboPay adapter do?
questions.explain: Cutting off a payment halfway creates exactly the unknown outcome you want to avoid. Waiting is safe because every call has a timeout, so stop always finishes.
options: stop refuses new charges and waits for the one in flight (which has its own timeout), then dispose aborts anything left

questions.q: A withLogging(inner) wrapper implements PaymentAdapter by forwarding to another adapter and logging each charge. What makes this possible?
questions.explain: This is the decorator pattern. Timing, metrics, circuit breakers and logging can all be wrappers, and every adapter stays a plain translator.
options: Checkout depends only on the PaymentAdapter interface, so anything that implements it, including a wrapper, can stand in

questions.q: The adapter translates KoboPay's answers. What does this print?
questions.explain: The adapter maps the provider's words to the contract's: failed becomes declined, and the reason is made readable. ?? supplies a default when the provider sends null, so checkout never shows "null" to a customer.
options:
{ status: 'declined', reason: 'card expired' }
{ status: 'declined', reason: null }

questions.q: Write a tiny registry: register(adapter) stores it under its trimmed, lower-cased name and throws Error("already registered: " + name) for a duplicate; require(name) finds it the same way or throws Error("not registered: " + name).
questions.explain: Normalizing the key in one helper, used by both methods, is what makes lookups case-insensitive and duplicates impossible. The stored adapter keeps its original name, as in AdapterRegistry.
questions.expected:
Fake-Payments
already registered: fake-payments
not registered: kobopay

questions.q: Finish the fake payment adapter's charge: return the stored result for a reference seen before; decline tok_declined with reason insufficient funds; otherwise succeed with chargeId: "fake_ch_" + n (n counts results stored so far, plus one).
questions.explain: A fake must keep the contract's promises too, idempotency included, or tests that use it prove nothing about the real adapters. Storing declines as well means a retried declined payment is not re-evaluated either.

questions.q: Write combine(reports): given an object of adapter name to { status }, return the worst status (unhealthy beats degraded beats healthy), and healthy for an empty object.
questions.explain: Ranking the statuses turns "the worst one" into a maximum. Treating an unknown status as unhealthy fails safe, the same choice healthAll makes.

questions.q: Write withTimeout(promise, ms, label): resolve with the promise's value, or reject with an Error named AdapterTimeoutError and the message <label> timed out after <ms>ms if it takes longer. Clear the timer either way.
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first. Note what it cannot do: the slow work keeps running in the background, which is why the real adapter also aborts the request with an AbortSignal. And the "charged" that arrives later is exactly the unknown outcome from the lesson.
questions.expected:
healthy
AdapterTimeoutError charge timed out after 50ms

questions.q: Write outcome(error) for checkout: "unknown" for an error named AdapterTimeoutError (the charge may have happened), "not charged" for AdapterConnectionError (the request never arrived), and "failed" for anything else.
questions.explain: The error class carries a fact the business needs: whether money may have moved. Only a timeout leaves that open. In the real code, use instanceof with the classes from @zudojs/adapters; the names here keep the exercise runnable anywhere.
questions.expected:
AdapterTimeoutError    unknown
AdapterConnectionError not charged
AdapterOperationError  failed
TypeError              failed

questions.q: Write disposeAll(adapters): for each adapter, call stop() then dispose() (both optional, maybe async). Run dispose even when stop throws, keep going with the other adapters, and at the end throw an AggregateError with every failure, if there were any.
questions.explain: Each step gets its own try, so one failure cannot skip the cleanup that follows. ?.() calls a hook only when the adapter has it. Collecting errors and throwing them together is what AdapterRegistry.disposeAll does.
questions.expected:
AggregateError [ 'pool busy' ]
stop database, dispose database, dispose payments, dispose sms

questions.q: Write cancelOrder(payments, chargeId): if payments.features.refunds is true, await payments.refund(chargeId) and return refunded <id>; otherwise return manual refund <id> via <name> without calling refund.
questions.explain: Checking the feature first turns a missing ability into a normal business path, instead of an exception. The adapter's AdapterNotSupportedError remains the safety net for code that forgets to check.
questions.expected:
refunded fake_ch_1
manual refund ch_7 via kobopay
